entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Amasis II (reigned c. 570–526 BCE), also known as Ahmose II, ascended to the throne of Egypt as a pharaoh of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty following a military revolt against his predecessor, Apries. His nearly 45-year reign, centered from the city of Sais in the Nile Delta, represented the last sustained period of native Egyptian strength and prosperity before the Achaemenid Persian conquest. Amasis skillfully navigated the complex geopolitical landscape of the Late Period, balancing alliances and rivalries with burgeoning Mediterranean powers like Lydia, Babylon, and the Greek city-states, thereby preserving Egyptian autonomy amidst escalating imperial ambitions.

Initially a general in the Egyptian army, Amasis seized power through a rebellion by native Egyptian troops dissatisfied with Apries' pro-Greek policies and military failures, notably against Cyrene. Once pharaoh, he consolidated his rule by reconciling with the powerful priestly class and implementing a strategic policy of economic growth through trade. He actively encouraged Greek merchants and artisans to settle in Naucratis, designating it as the sole port for foreign trade, which significantly boosted Egypt's economy. Militarily, Amasis secured Egypt's borders, notably by conquering Cyprus, incorporating the island into the Egyptian sphere of influence for the first time since the New Kingdom, and successfully repelling Babylonian incursions into Egyptian territory.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Amasis II was the last great native ruler of independent Egypt, whose long reign of nearly 45 years brought a final period of prosperity and stability before the Persian conquest. His diplomatic and economic policies shaped Egypt's interaction with the wider Mediterranean world, directly influencing the conditions of its eventual fall.
